引数の =hash= は =dissoc= に渡したキーのハッシュです。
保存されているキーと ~=~ になるのにハッシュが違うキーで =dissoc= すると、ノードに違うハッシュが記録されます。

ClojureではJavaの =ArrayList= と同じ要素のvectorは ~=~ になるのにハッシュが違います。
この食い違いは[[https://clojure.atlassian.net/browse/CLJ-1372][CLJ-1372]]で知られています。

次の例の =a= と =b= は、 =ArrayList= のハッシュがどちらも1003になるように選んだキーです。

#+begin_src clojure
(def a (java.util.ArrayList. [0 42]))
(def b (java.util.ArrayList. [1 11]))
[(hash a) (hash b) (hash [0 42]) (= a [0 42])]
;; => [1003 1003 1867155179 true]

(def m3 (-> (hash-map a :A b :B)
            (dissoc [0 42])
            (assoc a :A2)))
[m3 (count m3) (get m3 b)]
;; => [{[1 11] :B, [0 42] :A2} 2 nil]
#+end_src

=m3= を表示すると =b= のキーが見えるのに、 =(get m3 b)= は =nil= を返します。
=dissoc= のあとのノードには =[0 42]= のハッシュの1867155179が記録されるので、続く =assoc= は1003のキーと衝突しないと判断して2つを別の枝に分けます。

=b= を引くときは1003の枝をたどって =a= だけを見つけるので、 =b= は見つかりません。
この例では衝突ノードが木の1段目にあるので、 =dissoc= に渡すキーはハッシュの下位5bitが1003と同じである必要があり、1867155179はこの条件を満たしています。

[[./resources/public/img/8bda7e-hamt.svg]]

hash-setの =disj= でも同じことが起きて、transientの =dissoc!= を通る経路では起きません。

1.12.7の =PersistentHashMap.java= の該当行を =this.hash= に変えてコンパイルしました。
これをjarより先にclasspathに置いて同じ例を動かすと、 =(get m3 b)= は =:B= を返しました。

** 型ヒントの有無でremoveIfの結果が変わる
Clojure 1.12では、Javaのメソッドが関数型インターフェースを受け取るところにClojureの関数をそのまま渡せるようになりました。
このとき関数の返り値をClojureの真偽値として読む処理は、[[https://clojure.atlassian.net/browse/CLJ-2864][CLJ-2864]]で外されています。

#+begin_quote
In prior alphas, the FI adapter returns inserted Clojure truthy return logic when adapting a Clojure function to an FI with boolean return.
#+end_quote

コンパイラは型の分かる呼び出しにはこのとおりのコードを作りますが、型ヒントが無くてリフレクションを通る呼び出しは[[https://github.com/clojure/clojure/blob/clojure-1.12.7/src/jvm/clojure/lang/Reflector.java#L579-L591][Reflector.coerceAdapterReturn]]を使います。
そこでは =boolean= の返り値に =RT.booleanCast= を当てたままなので、同じ =.removeIf= の呼び出しが型ヒントの有無で別の結果になります。

#+begin_src clojure
(let [l (java.util.ArrayList. [1 2 3])]
  (.removeIf l #{1 2}) (vec l))
;; => ClassCastException
(let [l (identity (java.util.ArrayList. [1 2 3]))]
  (.removeIf l #{1 2}) (vec l))
;; => [3]
#+end_src

=identity= を挟むと =l= の型が分からなくなるので、呼び出しはリフレクションを通ります。

setを関数として渡すと要素そのものを返すので、型の分かる呼び出しは =Long= を =Boolean= にできずに例外を投げます。
リフレクションの呼び出しは返り値を真として読んで、要素を消します。

[[./resources/public/img/8bda7e-removeif.svg]]

** intのあふれとsubvecの負の添字
1.12には =drop= を速くした =IDrop= の実装があります。
そのうち文字列とvectorのseqの実装は、今の位置と =n= をintのまま足してから長さと比べています。
文字列のseqの[[https://github.com/clojure/clojure/blob/clojure-1.12.7/src/jvm/clojure/lang/StringSeq.java#L61-L68][StringSeq.drop]]もその1つです。

#+begin_src clojure
(drop Integer/MAX_VALUE (next (seq "abc")))
;; => StringIndexOutOfBoundsException Index -2147483648
(drop Integer/MAX_VALUE (seq "abc"))
;; => ()
#+end_src

Leanに写すと =i = 2147483646= と =n = 2147483647= の反例が出ました。
=n= を残りの長さ =s.length() - i= と比べる形に直すと、 =0 <= i < s.length()= と =0 < n= の前提の下で、32bitのすべての入力について素朴な仕様と一致することを証明できました。

[[./resources/public/img/8bda7e-drop.svg]]

=subvec= の結果への =assoc= では、[[https://github.com/clojure/clojure/blob/clojure-1.12.7/src/jvm/clojure/lang/APersistentVector.java#L661-L667][SubVector.assocN]]が負の添字を確かめていません。

#+begin_src clojure
(assoc [2 3] -1 :x)
;; => IndexOutOfBoundsException
(let [s (assoc (subvec [0 1 2 3 4] 2 4) -1 :x)]
  [s (.-v s)])
;; => [[2 3] [0 :x 2 3 4]]
#+end_src

subvecの外にある元のvectorの要素が書き換わって、見かけは変わらないsubvecが返ります。
=nth= の同じ不具合は[[https://clojure.atlassian.net/browse/CLJ-962][CLJ-962]]で直っているのですが、 =assoc= の側は直っていませんでした。

[[./resources/public/img/8bda7e-subvec.svg]]

** そのほかの候補
残りの12件は影響の小さいもので、どれもClojure 1.12.7で再現しています。

| 事象 | 例 |
|------+----|
| =reduce-kv= が =vector-of= で例外を投げる | =(reduce-kv f [] (vector-of :long 5 6))= |
| 引数3つ以上の関数型インターフェースで、型の分かる呼び出しのintの返り値が黙って切り詰められる | =(fn [a b c] 4294967297)= が1を返し、 =(fn [a b] 4294967297)= は =ArithmeticException= |
| 文字列やプリミティブ配列のseq、無限の =repeat= の =next= がメタデータを引き継ぐ | =(meta (rest (with-meta (seq "abc") {:m 1})))= が ={:m 1}= で、vectorのseqは =nil= |
| =(long ##NaN)= と =(int ##NaN)= が0を返す | =(long ##NaN)= が0で、 =(byte ##NaN)= は例外 |
| =long= がdoubleの2^63を、 =int= がfloatの2^31を最大値に丸める | =(long (Math/pow 2 63))= が =Long/MAX_VALUE= |
| =char= がBigIntを2^64で折り返す | =(char 18446744073709551681N)= が =\A= |
| =float= が =##Inf= を拒んで =##NaN= を通す | =(float ##Inf)= が例外で、 =(float ##NaN)= は =##NaN= |
| boxedとプリミティブのdoubleで、byteなどへの変換の範囲の判定が違う | =(byte (identity 127.9))= が127で、 =(byte 127.9)= は例外 |
| =get= が文字列とJavaの配列で小数の添字を切り詰める | =(get "abc" 1.9)= が =\b= |
| =byte-array= と =short-array= が初期値を受け付けない | =(byte-array 2 7)= が例外 |
| プリミティブ配列のseqで =.indexOf= と =.contains= が食い違う | =(.indexOf (seq (byte-array [1 2 3])) 2)= が-1 |
| listの =.lastIndexOf= が ~=~ でなく =equals= で比べる | =(.lastIndexOf (list 1 2) (int 2))= が-1 |

** 見つからなかったところ
=PersistentHashMap= と =PersistentHashSet= は、永続とtransientの操作を混ぜた300万回の操作で =java.util.HashMap= と食い違いませんでした。
更新する前のmapが変わらないことや、 =ArrayNode= の分割と統合、深さ7までの衝突ノードも見ています。

=PersistentTreeMap= も =java.util.TreeMap= と食い違わずに赤黒木の条件を保っていました。
vectorの木の境界の前後でも =ArrayList= との食い違いは出ませんでした。

数値の側では、 =Numbers= の足し算と引き算が速い経路を選ぶ判定はオーバーフローの判定と一致することを64bitで証明できました。

掛け算は =bv_decide= が16bitで時間切れになるので8bitと10bitで確かめています。
=clojure.core/mod= が床関数の剰余と一致することは32bitまで証明しました。

Leanで証明した性質はどれも記事に書いたモデルの上で成り立つものです。
モデルが実際のJavaのコードと同じ意味かは、ソースと再現の結果を突き合わせて確かめています。

* I checked Clojure's core with Lean and differential testing and found unreported bugs in HAMT and vector-of
:properties:
:export_file_name: generated/contents/blog/2026/e4f733
:export_original: /blog/2026/8bda7e
:export_date: 2026-11-24 12:16
:export_updated: 2026-11-24 12:16
:export_lang: en
:export_tags: clojure lean formal-verification testing differential-testing
:end:

I read Koukyosyumei's article "[[https://zenn.dev/koukyosyumei/articles/31c8fcf4da45b7][著名なRust製OSSをLean 4で形式検証してみたら、めちゃめちゃバグが見つかった話]]" (in Japanese; the title means "I formally verified well-known Rust OSS with Lean 4 and found a lot of bugs").
The author ported well-known Rust projects into a form they could prove in Lean 4, and where a proof failed, they found a bug in the original code.

Many people have used Clojure's persistent data structures since around 1.0, so I expected no bugs to remain.
Still, I wanted to see whether Lean would find something there too.

[[https://github.com/hirosassa/lean-verify][hirosassa/lean-verify]] describes a procedure for modeling a small function in Lean 4 and checking it for all inputs, so I applied it to the part of Clojure's core written in Java.

I modeled integer and bit arithmetic in Lean and searched for counterexamples.
I checked the collections with differential testing against the =java.util= collections, and for Java interop I compared the same call with and without a type hint.

I found 17 bugs that I could not find in Clojure's JIRA or on ask.clojure.org.
They include =reduce= on =vector-of=, the hash collision node of the HAMT, and calls to functional interfaces without a type hint.

The HAMT itself showed no mismatch in 3 million operations of differential testing, and the vector tree showed none around its boundaries.
The bugs sat in separate code outside the trees, and in places where two mechanisms meet, such as ~=~ and hashing.

I used Clojure 1.12.7, released on 2026-11-18, and JDK 21.
The links to the source point to the [[https://github.com/clojure/clojure/tree/clojure-1.12.7][clojure-1.12.7]] tag.

** How I checked
The lean-verify procedure picks one function and models it as a Lean definition.
You write a property that compares it with a naive specification computed at a wider width, and =bv_decide= searches for a counterexample.

If you model Java's =long= and =int= as =BitVec 64= and =BitVec 32=, the wraparound of addition and multiplication maps onto =BitVec= operations.
So do the rounding of =/= toward zero and the sign of =%=.

When Lean found a counterexample, I turned the value into a Clojure input and reproduced it in the original code.
I then modeled the fixed code in Lean and proved the same property.
Lean can only take small functions that reduce to integer and bit arithmetic, so I checked the large persistent data structures with differential testing.

Each test applies the same random sequence of operations to =PersistentHashMap= and to =java.util.HashMap= and compares the results.
For the HAMT, the keys mix partial collisions at each 5-bit level with fully identical hashes, and I ran 1,500 operations for each of 2,000 seeds.

For vectors, I compared against =ArrayList= around 32, 1056, 32800, and 1048608, where the tree gains a level.
The operations were =conj=, =pop=, =assoc=, and their transient versions.

I checked whether anyone had reported each bug before.
I searched Clojure's JIRA through its REST API and ask.clojure.org through web search and the site's own search, and found no matching report.

** reduce on vector-of never finishes
=vector-of= is a vector that stores its values in primitive arrays.
Clojure implements it in =gvec.clj=, written in Clojure and separate from =PersistentVector=.
If you =drop= from one and then =reduce= it, the call never returns once the vector has 65505 or more elements.

#+begin_src clojure
(reduce + (drop 1 (into (vector-of :long) (range 65504))))
;; => 2145354256
(reduce + (drop 1 (into (vector-of :long) (range 65505))))
;; => never returns
(reduce + (drop 1 (vec (range 65505))))
;; => 2145419760
#+end_src

The cause is [[https://github.com/clojure/clojure/blob/clojure-1.12.7/src/clj/clojure/gvec.clj#L79][line 79 of gvec.clj]], where the seq's =reduce= computes the start of the next 32-element chunk.

#+begin_src clojure
(recur result (bit-and 0xffe0 (+ aidx 32)))
#+end_src

The code uses =0xffe0= to clear the low 5 bits and round down to a multiple of 32, but the mask also clears bit 16 and everything above it.
With 65505 elements, the last chunk starts at index 65504.
After that chunk, the start of the next one should be 65536, but the mask turns it into 0, so =reduce= goes back to the start and reads the vector again and again.

[[./resources/public/img/e4f733-mask.svg]]

The =0xffe0= mask has stayed in place since the [[https://github.com/clojure/clojure/commit/5b281880][2010 commit]] that added =internal-reduce=.
In Lean, I wrote the property that from a position =a= that is a multiple of 32, the next chunk starts at =a + 32=.

#+begin_src lean
import Std.Tactic.BVDecide

def stepImpl (a : BitVec 64) : BitVec 64 := 0xffe0 &&& (a + 32)
def stepFix (a : BitVec 64) : BitVec 64 := (~~~0x1f) &&& (a + 32)

theorem impl_ok (a : BitVec 64) (h32 : a &&& 0x1f = 0) (hlt : a < 0x7fffffe0) :
    stepImpl a = a + 32 := by
  unfold stepImpl; bv_decide
theorem fix_ok (a : BitVec 64) (h32 : a &&& 0x1f = 0) (hlt : a < 0x7fffffe0) :
    stepFix a = a + 32 := by
  unfold stepFix; bv_decide
#+end_src

=impl_ok= fails with the counterexample =a = 1073741792=, and =#eval stepImpl 65504= returns 0 as well.
=fix_ok= uses =(bit-not 0x1f)= as the mask, and its proof goes through under the assumption that =a= is a multiple of 32 below =0x7fffffe0=.

** dissoc on a HAMT collision node hides another key
Clojure's hash-map is a HAMT: it splits the key's hash into 5-bit pieces and uses them to walk down the tree.
Keys whose 32-bit hashes are identical share a =HashCollisionNode= at the bottom of the tree, and the node finds a key among them with ~=~.

[[https://github.com/clojure/clojure/blob/clojure-1.12.7/src/jvm/clojure/lang/PersistentHashMap.java#L964-L971][HashCollisionNode.without]] builds the new node with one key removed.
It should give the new node its own hash, =this.hash=, but it passes the parameter =hash= instead.

#+begin_src java
return new HashCollisionNode(null, hash, count - 1, removePair(array, idx/2));
#+end_src

The parameter =hash= is the hash of the key you pass to =dissoc=.
If you =dissoc= with a key that is ~=~ to the stored key but has a different hash, the node records the wrong hash.

In Clojure, a vector is ~=~ to a Java =ArrayList= with the same elements, but the two hash differently.
[[https://clojure.atlassian.net/browse/CLJ-1372][CLJ-1372]] tracks this mismatch.

In the example below, I chose =a= and =b= so that both =ArrayList= keys hash to 1003.

#+begin_src clojure
(def a (java.util.ArrayList. [0 42]))
(def b (java.util.ArrayList. [1 11]))
[(hash a) (hash b) (hash [0 42]) (= a [0 42])]
;; => [1003 1003 1867155179 true]

(def m3 (-> (hash-map a :A b :B)
            (dissoc [0 42])
            (assoc a :A2)))
[m3 (count m3) (get m3 b)]
;; => [{[1 11] :B, [0 42] :A2} 2 nil]
#+end_src

When you print =m3=, you can see the key =b=, but =(get m3 b)= returns =nil=.
After the =dissoc=, the node records 1867155179, the hash of =[0 42]=.
The next =assoc= then concludes that =a=, with hash 1003, does not collide with the node, and splits the two into separate branches.

A lookup of =b= follows the branch for 1003 and finds only =a= there, so it never reaches =b=.
In this example the collision node sits on the first level of the tree, so the key passed to =dissoc= needs the same low 5 bits as 1003, and 1867155179 has them.

[[./resources/public/img/e4f733-hamt.svg]]

=disj= on a hash-set has the same bug, while the path through the transient =dissoc!= does not.

I changed that line in the 1.12.7 =PersistentHashMap.java= to =this.hash= and compiled it.
With the patched class ahead of the jar on the classpath, the same example returned =:B= for =(get m3 b)=.

** removeIf gives different results with and without a type hint
Since Clojure 1.12, you can pass a Clojure function directly where a Java method takes a functional interface.
[[https://clojure.atlassian.net/browse/CLJ-2864][CLJ-2864]] removed the logic that read the function's return value as a Clojure truthy value.

#+begin_quote
In prior alphas, the FI adapter returns inserted Clojure truthy return logic when adapting a Clojure function to an FI with boolean return.
#+end_quote

The compiler follows this for calls where it knows the type.
A call without a type hint goes through reflection and uses [[https://github.com/clojure/clojure/blob/clojure-1.12.7/src/jvm/clojure/lang/Reflector.java#L579-L591][Reflector.coerceAdapterReturn]].
That method still applies =RT.booleanCast= to a =boolean= return value, so the same =.removeIf= call gives a different result depending on the type hint.

#+begin_src clojure
(let [l (java.util.ArrayList. [1 2 3])]
  (.removeIf l #{1 2}) (vec l))
;; => ClassCastException
(let [l (identity (java.util.ArrayList. [1 2 3]))]
  (.removeIf l #{1 2}) (vec l))
;; => [3]
#+end_src

Wrapping the list in =identity= hides the type of =l=, so the call goes through reflection.

A set used as a function returns the element itself.
In the call with a known type, the adapter cannot turn the =Long= into a =Boolean= and throws.
The reflective call reads the return value as true and removes the elements.

[[./resources/public/img/e4f733-removeif.svg]]

** int overflow and a negative subvec index
Clojure 1.12 added =IDrop= implementations that make =drop= faster.
The ones for string seqs and vector seqs add the current position and =n= as ints and then compare the sum with the length.
[[https://github.com/clojure/clojure/blob/clojure-1.12.7/src/jvm/clojure/lang/StringSeq.java#L61-L68][StringSeq.drop]] for string seqs is one of them.

#+begin_src clojure
(drop Integer/MAX_VALUE (next (seq "abc")))
;; => StringIndexOutOfBoundsException Index -2147483648
(drop Integer/MAX_VALUE (seq "abc"))
;; => ()
#+end_src

The Lean model gave the counterexample =i = 2147483646= and =n = 2147483647=.
I changed the check to compare =n= with the remaining length =s.length() - i=.
Under the assumptions =0 <= i < s.length()= and =0 < n=, Lean proved that the fixed check matches the naive specification for every 32-bit input.

[[./resources/public/img/e4f733-drop.svg]]

For =assoc= on the result of =subvec=, [[https://github.com/clojure/clojure/blob/clojure-1.12.7/src/jvm/clojure/lang/APersistentVector.java#L661-L667][SubVector.assocN]] does not reject a negative index.

#+begin_src clojure
(assoc [2 3] -1 :x)
;; => IndexOutOfBoundsException
(let [s (assoc (subvec [0 1 2 3 4] 2 4) -1 :x)]
  [s (.-v s)])
;; => [[2 3] [0 :x 2 3 4]]
#+end_src

The call overwrites an element of the underlying vector outside the subvec, and returns a subvec that looks unchanged.
[[https://clojure.atlassian.net/browse/CLJ-962][CLJ-962]] fixed the same bug in =nth=, but =assoc= still has it.

[[./resources/public/img/e4f733-subvec.svg]]

** Other findings
The other 12 bugs have a smaller impact, and I reproduced each of them on Clojure 1.12.7.

| Behavior | Example |
|------+----|
| =reduce-kv= throws on =vector-of= | =(reduce-kv f [] (vector-of :long 5 6))= |
| With a functional interface of three or more arguments, a call with a known type truncates an =int= return value without an error | =(fn [a b c] 4294967297)= returns 1, and =(fn [a b] 4294967297)= throws =ArithmeticException= |
| =next= on a seq of a string, a primitive array, or an infinite =repeat= keeps the metadata | =(meta (rest (with-meta (seq "abc") {:m 1})))= is ={:m 1}=, and for a vector's seq it is =nil= |
| =(long ##NaN)= and =(int ##NaN)= return 0 | =(long ##NaN)= is 0, and =(byte ##NaN)= throws |
| =long= clamps a double 2^63, and =int= a float 2^31, to the maximum value | =(long (Math/pow 2 63))= is =Long/MAX_VALUE= |
| =char= wraps a BigInt at 2^64 | =(char 18446744073709551681N)= is =\A= |
| =float= rejects =##Inf= but lets =##NaN= through | =(float ##Inf)= throws, and =(float ##NaN)= is =##NaN= |
| Boxed and primitive doubles use different range checks when converted to byte and similar types | =(byte (identity 127.9))= is 127, and =(byte 127.9)= throws |
| =get= truncates a fractional index on strings and Java arrays | =(get "abc" 1.9)= is =\b= |
| =byte-array= and =short-array= reject an initial value | =(byte-array 2 7)= throws |
| On a seq of a primitive array, =.indexOf= and =.contains= disagree | =(.indexOf (seq (byte-array [1 2 3])) 2)= is -1 |
| =.lastIndexOf= on a list compares with =equals= instead of ~=~ | =(.lastIndexOf (list 1 2) (int 2))= is -1 |

** Where I found nothing
=PersistentHashMap= and =PersistentHashSet= matched =java.util.HashMap= over 3 million operations that mixed persistent and transient updates.
The tests also covered maps before an update staying unchanged, =ArrayNode= splits and merges, and collision nodes down to depth 7.

=PersistentTreeMap= matched =java.util.TreeMap= and kept the red-black tree invariants.
Vectors matched =ArrayList= around every tree boundary I tested.

On the numeric side, Lean proved for 64 bits that the check =Numbers= uses to pick the fast path for addition and subtraction agrees with the overflow check.

For multiplication, =bv_decide= timed out at 16 bits, so I checked 8 and 10 bits.
I proved up to 32 bits that =clojure.core/mod= matches the floored remainder.

Every property I proved in Lean holds for the model shown in this article.
I checked that each model means the same thing as the Java code by comparing it with the source and with the reproduced behavior.

* Lean 4で証明した関数をGoから呼べて、Goの関数をLeanで証明できるleanfranのGo版を作った
:properties:
:export_file_name: generated/contents/blog/2026/ad14a8
:export_date: 2026-11-25 05:00
:export_updated: 2026-11-26 07:51
:export_tags: lean go formal-verification code-generation release lean-leanfran
:end:
Lean 4で書いて証明した関数をGoのパッケージから呼べるようにするleanfranのGo版を作りました。
逆向きに、Goで書いた関数をLeanに訳してその性質をLeanで証明することもできます。

Leanのstructureは値を作るときにフィールドの条件を検査するGoのstructになり、列挙や場合分けを表す帰納型もGoの型になります。

リポジトリは[[https://github.com/conao3/lean-leanfran/tree/v0.13.2/langs/Go][conao3/lean-leanfranのlangs/Go/]]で、ライセンスはApache-2.0です。
Goのmoduleは[[https://pkg.go.dev/github.com/conao3/leanfran-go@v0.13.2][github.com/conao3/leanfran-go]]の名前で公開していて、この記事は0.13.2で動かした結果をもとに書いています。

leanfranはLeanのコンパイラの中間表現をGoに変換するものです。
生成したGoはこのmoduleとGoの標準ライブラリだけで動き、実行するときにLeanもcgoも要りません。

Rust・Python・TypeScript・Clojureの4つは[[https://s.conao3.com/blog/2026/23d62c][leanfranを紹介した記事]]で、PHPは[[https://s.conao3.com/blog/2026/ec8faf][PHP版の記事]]で取り上げています。
Go版も同じリポジトリから同じ版で出しています。

[[github:conao3/lean-leanfran::Lean][Write and prove functions in Lean 4, run them as Rust, Python, TypeScript, Clojure, PHP and Go]]

** 4つの使い方
leanfranをGoから使う方法は4つあります。

[[./resources/public/img/ad14a8-uses.svg]]

1. Goのパッケージの =leanfran.Lean(...)= の引数にLeanの関数と定理を書き、 =go tool leanfran sync= で生成した関数をGoから呼ぶ。
2. Leanのstructureと帰納型を、値の検査とJSONの変換が付いたGoの型として使う。
3. Leanの値を =leanfran.Value[T]= でGoの変数に持ち続け、次の呼び出しに変換せずに渡す。
4. Goで書いた関数に =//leanfran:model= を付けてLeanに訳し、 =go tool leanfran check= で関数の性質を証明したLeanの定理を検査する。

1から3はLeanからGoへ、4はGoからLeanへの向きです。

** GoのパッケージにLeanを書く
Leanを変換するCLIの =leanfran-go= はnixで入れ、アプリケーションのmoduleにはleanfran-goのパッケージと =go tool= で呼ぶコマンドを足します。

#+begin_src console
$ nix profile install github:conao3/lean-leanfran/v0.13.2#go
$ go mod init example.com/shop
$ go get github.com/conao3/leanfran-go@v0.13.2
$ go get -tool github.com/conao3/leanfran-go/cmd/leanfran@v0.13.2
#+end_src

Goは1.26以上が要ります。
生成と証明の検査にはLean 4.35.0の =lean= と =lake= も =PATH= に要ります。

=pricing/pricing.go= に次のパッケージを書きます。

#+begin_src go
package pricing

import "github.com/conao3/leanfran-go"

var _ = leanfran.Lean(`
structure Range where
  lo : Nat
  hi : Nat
  ok : lo ≤ hi

def width (r : Range) : Nat := r.hi - r.lo

theorem width_le (r : Range) : width r ≤ r.hi := by
  unfold width
  omega
`)
#+end_src

=leanfran.Lean(...)= にはLeanのソースをraw stringで書き、この記事では =leanfran.Lean(...)= に渡したLeanをブロックと呼びます。
ブロックは1つのパッケージに1つ置きます。

=Range= の =ok= は =lo ≤ hi= が成り立つことを表すフィールドです。
=width_le= は幅が上限を超えないという定理です。

呼び出す側の =main.go= では、生成される =NewRange= で値を作って =pricing.Width= に渡します。

#+begin_src go
package main

import (
	"fmt"
	"log"
	"math/big"

	"example.com/shop/pricing"
)

func main() {
	r, err := pricing.NewRange(big.NewInt(2), big.NewInt(5))
	if err != nil {
		log.Fatal(err)
	}
	width, err := pricing.Width(r)
	if err != nil {
		log.Fatal(err)
	}
	fmt.Println(width)
}
#+end_src

=go tool leanfran sync= を実行するとLeanが定理を検査し、leanfranがGoを生成するので、そのあとはGoだけでビルドして実行できます。

#+begin_src console
$ go tool leanfran sync
leanfran: 1 block checked and generated
$ go run .
3
#+end_src

=sync= はブロックのハッシュを記録した =leanfran.json= と生成したGoのファイルを =pricing.go= と同じディレクトリに置きます。
これらをリポジトリにcommitしておけば、CIではLeanを入れずに =go tool leanfran status= で古くなっていないかを確かめられます。

定理を =width r ≤ r.lo= に書き換えると証明が通らなくなり、生成はそこで止まります。

#+begin_src console
$ go tool leanfran sync 2>&1 | sed "s|$PWD/||"
leanfran: lake build: exit status 1
✖ [4/6] Building LeanGoEmbed.B6578616d706c652e636f6d2f73686f702f70726963696e67 (263ms)
pricing/pricing.go:15:3: error: (lean block example.com/shop/pricing, Lean 11:2) omega could not prove the goal:
a possible counterexample may satisfy the constraints
  b ≥ 0
  a ≥ 0
  a - b ≤ 0
  2*a - b ≤ -1
where
 a := ↑r.lo
 b := ↑r.hi
Some required targets logged failures:
- LeanGoEmbed.B6578616d706c652e636f6d2f73686f702f70726963696e67
error: build failed
#+end_src

エラーはGoのファイルの行と列から始まり、そのあとにブロックの中のLeanの行と列が続きます。
生成に失敗したときは前に生成したGoが残るので、 =go run .= はこのあとも =3= を出力します。

** Leanの型がGoの型になる
=Range= はGoのstructになり、 =lo= と =hi= は =*big.Int= 型のフィールドの =Lo= と =Hi= になります。
=ok= は値を作るときの =lo ≤ hi= の検査になります。

次の =cmd/rangecheck/main.go= ではJSONから値を作り、条件を満たさない入力を =NewRange= に渡してから、JSON Schemaを出力しています。

#+begin_src go
package main

import (
	"encoding/json"
	"fmt"
	"log"
	"math/big"

	"example.com/shop/pricing"
)

func main() {
	var r pricing.Range
	if err := json.Unmarshal([]byte(`{"lo":1,"hi":4}`), &r); err != nil {
		log.Fatal(err)
	}
	fmt.Println(r.Hi)

	_, err := pricing.NewRange(big.NewInt(5), big.NewInt(2))
	fmt.Println(err)

	schema, err := r.JSONSchema("draft-2020-12")
	if err != nil {
		log.Fatal(err)
	}
	out, _ := json.MarshalIndent(schema, "", "  ")
	fmt.Println(string(out))
}
#+end_src

#+begin_src console
$ go run ./cmd/rangecheck
4
Range.ok: lo ≤ hi
{
  "$schema": "https://json-schema.org/draft/2020-12/schema",
  "additionalProperties": false,
  "properties": {
    "hi": {
      "minimum": 0,
      "type": "integer"
    },
    "lo": {
      "minimum": 0,
      "type": "integer"
    }
  },
  "required": [
    "lo",
    "hi"
  ],
  "type": "object"
}
#+end_src

=NewRange= はLeanからコンパイルしたコードで =lo ≤ hi= を判定するので、 =lo= が =hi= より大きい値を渡すと =*leanfran.ValidationError= を返します。
JSON Schemaでは2つのフィールドにまたがる =lo ≤ hi= を表せないので、schemaには =Nat= が0以上であることだけが出ます。

=json.Unmarshal= と =Validate= も =NewRange= と同じ条件を検査します。
生成した関数も引数を受け取ったときに検査するので、structリテラルで作った値を =pricing.Width= に渡しても =*leanfran.ValidationError= が返ります。

** Leanの値をGoで持ち続ける
生成した関数は呼び出しのたびに引数をLeanの表現に変換し、戻り値をGoの値に変換します。
大きな値を繰り返し渡すと、この変換が実行時間の大半を占めます。

=leanfran.Value[T]= はLeanの値への参照を1つ持つhandleです。
handleを使うと、Leanの値を変換せずにGoの変数に置いておけます。

=ledger/ledger.go= に、配列に金額を1件足す =record= と件数を返す =count= を書きます。

#+begin_src go
package ledger

import "github.com/conao3/leanfran-go"

var _ = leanfran.Lean(`
def record (xs : Array UInt64) (x : UInt64) : Array UInt64 := xs.push x

def count (xs : Array UInt64) : Nat := xs.size

theorem count_record (xs : Array UInt64) (x : UInt64) :
    count (record xs x) = count xs + 1 := by
  simp [count, record]
`)
#+end_src

=sync= は =[]uint64= を受け取る =Record= と一緒に、handleを受け取ってhandleを返す =Handle.Record= も生成します。
Goの値とhandleの変換には、 =ledger.Value.NewArrayUInt64= や =ledger.Value.ReadNat= のように、生成される =ledger.Value= のメソッドを使います。

次の =cmd/ledger/main.go= では最初の2件をGoのスライスからhandleにして、そのあとの2件はhandleの =entries= に足しています。
=record= と =count= は引数を検査せず、Lean側でも失敗しないので、生成される関数は =error= を返しません。

#+begin_src go
package main

import (
	"fmt"

	"example.com/shop/ledger"
)

func main() {
	entries := ledger.Value.NewArrayUInt64([]uint64{1200, 800})
	defer func() { entries.Close() }()

	for _, amount := range []uint64{300, 50} {
		x := ledger.Value.NewUInt64(amount)
		entries = ledger.Handle.Record(entries.Take(), x.Take())
	}

	n := ledger.Handle.Count(entries.Borrow())
	defer n.Close()
	fmt.Println(ledger.Value.ReadNat(n))
	fmt.Println(ledger.Value.ReadArrayUInt64(entries))
}
#+end_src

#+begin_src console
$ go tool leanfran sync
leanfran: 2 blocks checked and generated
$ go run ./cmd/ledger
4
[1200 800 300 50]
#+end_src

引数には =entries.Borrow()= か =entries.Take()= を渡します。
=Borrow= は呼び出しのあとも =entries= を使い続けるとき、 =Take= は参照ごとLeanに渡して、そのhandleを使い終えるときに使います。

=Take= で渡した配列にはほかに参照が無いので、Leanの =Array.push= は配列をコピーせずにその場で1件足します。

=Value.ReadNat= と =Value.ReadArrayUInt64= がhandleの中身をGoの値に変換するメソッドです。
使い終えたhandleは =Close= を呼んで参照を手放します。
GoのGCはこの参照を手放さないので、 =Take= で渡さなかったhandleには =Close= を呼びます。

10件と1,000件と100,000件の配列に1件足す操作を、Linux・amd64のIntel Core i5-8400とGo 1.27.3で測りました。
=Record= には同じスライスを毎回渡し、 =Handle.Record= には同じ件数の配列で作ったhandleを =Take= で渡し続けています。

図と表の値は、CPUを1つに固定して11回測った時間の中央値から求めた1秒あたりの回数で、大きいほど速いことを表します。

[[./resources/public/img/ad14a8-record.svg]]

| 配列の件数 | =Record= (回/秒) | =Handle.Record= (回/秒) |
|---+---+---|
| 10 | 2,520,000 | 7,000,000 |
| 1,000 | 63,800 | 7,100,000 |
| 100,000 | 534 | 6,970,000 |

=Record= は配列の件数が増えるほど回数が減りますが、 =Handle.Record= は件数によらず毎秒697万回から710万回です。

handleはどれも1つの領域に属し、leanfran-goのランタイムは同じ領域のhandleの操作を1つずつ順に実行します。
ここまでの例のhandleは、プロセスに1つある既定の領域に属します。
=leanfran.NewRegion()= で領域を作り、その領域の =WithValues= の中でhandleを作ると、別々の領域のhandleを複数のgoroutineから同時に操作できます。

サーバーが状態をhandleで持ち、リクエストごとに次の状態のhandleへ置き換える使い方は[[https://github.com/conao3/lean-leanfran/tree/v0.13.2/langs/Go/samples/value-server][value-serverのサンプル]]にあります。

** Goの関数をLeanで証明する
逆向きの例として、値を範囲に収める =Clamp= をGoで書き、 =//leanfran:model= でLeanの仕様と結びつけます。

#+begin_src go
package calc

import "github.com/conao3/leanfran-go"

var _ = leanfran.Lean(`
def clampSpec (x lo hi : Int64) : Int64 := max lo (min hi x)
def ordered (_x lo hi : Int64) : Bool := decide (lo ≤ hi)
def inRange (_x lo hi r : Int64) : Bool := decide (lo ≤ r) && decide (r ≤ hi)
`)

//leanfran:model refines=clampSpec requires=ordered ensures=in_range:inRange
func Clamp(x, lo, hi int64) int64 {
	if x < lo {
		return lo
	}
	if x > hi {
		return hi
	}
	return x
}
#+end_src

=refines= には実装と同じ値を返すLeanの関数、 =requires= には入力の前提、 =ensures= には戻り値が満たす条件を書きます。
この例では =lo ≤ hi= のときに =Clamp= が =clampSpec= と同じ値を返すことと、戻り値が =lo= 以上 =hi= 以下になることが証明の義務です。

=go tool leanfran check= はGoの構文木と型を読んで関数をLeanの関数に訳し、 =Clamp.obligation.refines= のような名前で義務の命題を作ります。
証明は =go.mod= の隣の =lean/Proofs/= に書き、ここでは[[https://github.com/conao3/lean-leanfran/blob/v0.13.2/langs/Go/samples/verified-clamp/lean/Proofs/Clamp.lean][verified-clampのサンプルの証明]]のモジュール名だけをこのパッケージに合わせています。

#+begin_src lean
import LeanGoModel.B6578616d706c652e636f6d2f73686f702f63616c63

open LeanGoEmbed.B6578616d706c652e636f6d2f73686f702f63616c63
namespace LeanGoModel.B6578616d706c652e636f6d2f73686f702f63616c63

theorem Clamp.proof.refines : Clamp.obligation.refines := by
  intro x lo hi h
  simp only [ordered, decide_eq_true_eq] at h
  simp only [Clamp, clampSpec, Id.run, pure, Pure.pure, Int64.min_def, Int64.max_def,
    decide_eq_true_eq]
  repeat' split
  all_goals simp_all only [Int64.lt_iff_toInt_lt, Int64.le_iff_toInt_le, ← Int64.toInt_inj] <;> omega

theorem Clamp.proof.in_range : Clamp.obligation.in_range := by
  intro x lo hi h
  simp only [ordered, decide_eq_true_eq] at h
  simp only [Clamp, inRange, Id.run, pure, Pure.pure, Bool.and_eq_true, decide_eq_true_eq]
  split <;> try split
  all_goals simp_all only [Int64.lt_iff_toInt_lt, Int64.le_iff_toInt_le]
  all_goals constructor <;> first | exact True.intro | omega

end LeanGoModel.B6578616d706c652e636f6d2f73686f702f63616c63
#+end_src

モジュール名の =B= に続く部分は、Goのimport pathの =example.com/shop/calc= をUTF-8のバイトごとに16進数で書いたものです。

#+begin_src console
$ go tool leanfran check --require proved
leanfran: 3 blocks checked and generated
example.com/shop/calc.Clamp [in_range]: proved
example.com/shop/calc.Clamp [refines]: proved
#+end_src

=--require proved= を付けると、義務が1つでも =proved= でなければ終了コードが1になります。
=proved= は定理の型が義務と一致していて、証明を省く =sorry= やLeanの標準にない公理に頼っていないことを表します。

=check= は義務ごとの結果を =go.mod= の隣の =leanfran.lock= に書くので、これもcommitしておけば =go tool leanfran status= でLeanを入れずに証明の結果が古くなっていないかを確かめられます。

Goの実装とLeanの仕様は乱数で作った入力を使うテストでも比べられ、このテストはLeanなしで動きます。
=sync= は =//leanfran:model= のあるパッケージに =leanfran_model_test.go= を生成するので、 =go test= で実行できます。

#+begin_src console
$ go test ./calc/
ok  	example.com/shop/calc	0.003s
#+end_src

生成されるテストはシードを固定した乱数と、0や整数の上限などの境界の値で入力を作り、 =requires= を満たす入力を200件集めます。
その入力ごとに、Goの =Clamp= の戻り値を =clampSpec= から生成した =ClampSpec= の値と比べます。

実装の2つめの =if= を、 =x= が =hi= 以上のときに =hi - 1= を返すように書き換えてみます。

#+begin_src go
	if x >= hi {
		return hi - 1
	}
#+end_src

2つの証明が通らなくなるので、 =check= はLeanのエラーを標準エラー出力に出したうえで、義務ごとの状態を =failed= にします。

#+begin_src console
$ go tool leanfran check --require proved 2>/dev/null
leanfran: 3 blocks checked and generated
example.com/shop/calc.Clamp [in_range]: failed
example.com/shop/calc.Clamp [refines]: failed
#+end_src

=go test= で動かす乱数のテストも、3つの引数がすべて0の入力で反例を見つけます。

#+begin_src console
$ go test ./calc/
--- FAIL: TestLeanfranModels (0.00s)
    --- FAIL: TestLeanfranModels/Clamp (0.00s)
        leanfran_model_test.go:12: Clamp: refines: got []interface {}{-1}, want []interface {}{0} (seed=1, input=[]interface {}{0, 0, 0})
FAIL
FAIL	example.com/shop/calc	0.002s
FAIL
#+end_src

** 証明が保証する範囲
Leanの定理はLeanで書いた関数とGoから訳したLeanのモデルの性質を保証します。
生成したGoや元のGoの実行にもその性質が成り立つには、LeanをGoに変換する生成器とランタイム、GoをLeanに訳す翻訳器とGoの演算のモデルが正しい必要があるので、この4つはテストで確かめています。

翻訳器は手で書いたGoを実行した結果と、訳したモデルをLeanの標準のCバックエンドでコンパイルして動かした結果を比べるテストで確かめています。
演算のモデルはモデルから生成したコードとGoの演算を境界の値で比べ、モデルの失敗とGoの =panic= が対応することも見ています。

LeanをGoに変換する生成器とランタイムは、生成したGoの結果をLeanのCバックエンドの結果と比べるテストで確かめています。

この記事を書いた時点で、Linux・amd64では境界の値と乱数で作った1,769,817件の数値の演算を試しました。
そのうち1,764,071件の結果がCバックエンドの結果とバイト単位で一致しています。

残りの5,746件は浮動小数点数を返す関数のもので、差は関数ごとに決めた幅に収まっています。
=Float.cos= は差が最も大きく、隣り合う浮動小数点数の間隔の88個分です。

GoをLeanに訳すときには、Goの整数を同じ幅のLeanの整数にして、 =int= と =uint= は =Int64= と =UInt64= にします。
ゼロ除算と範囲外の添字と =panic= は、モデルの上では失敗を表す値になります。

訳せるのはGoの一部で、 =if= ・ =switch= ・ =for= 、スライスの添字と =append= 、structを扱えます。

ポインタ・map・channel・goroutine・メソッド・generics・ =defer= ・入出力を含む関数は対象外です。
対応する構文の一覧は[[https://github.com/conao3/lean-leanfran/blob/v0.13.2/docs/go-guide.md#go-subset-and-proof-scope][Goのガイド]]にあります。

** おわりに
この記事の例のほかにも、[[https://github.com/conao3/lean-leanfran/tree/v0.13.2/langs/Go/samples][Goのサンプル]]にはビットマスクと剰余が等しいことを証明するverified-nibbleを置いてあります。
2つのパッケージでGoのstructを共有するembed-modelsや、Leanの =IO= の関数をGoのコマンドとして動かすgreet-cliもあります。

導入の手順は[[https://github.com/conao3/lean-leanfran/blob/v0.13.2/langs/Go/README.md][GoのREADME]]、型の対応やCLIの詳細は[[https://github.com/conao3/lean-leanfran/blob/v0.13.2/docs/go-guide.md][Goのガイド]]にあります。

* leanfran for Go: call Lean 4 functions from Go, and prove Go functions in Lean
:properties:
:export_file_name: generated/contents/blog/2026/3b66b5
:export_date: 2026-11-27 20:22
:export_updated: 2026-11-27 20:22
:export_draft: t
:export_lang: en
:export_original: /blog/2026/ad14a8
:export_tags: lean go formal-verification code-generation release lean-leanfran
:end:
I built the Go version of leanfran, which lets you call functions written and proved in Lean 4 from Go packages.
In the other direction, you can translate functions written in Go into Lean and prove their properties in Lean.

A Lean structure becomes a Go struct that checks its field conditions when you create a value, and inductive types for enumerations and case splits become Go types too.

The repository is [[https://github.com/conao3/lean-leanfran/tree/v0.13.2/langs/Go][langs/Go/ in conao3/lean-leanfran]], under the Apache-2.0 license.
I publish the Go module as [[https://pkg.go.dev/github.com/conao3/leanfran-go@v0.13.2][github.com/conao3/leanfran-go]], and this post uses the results of running version 0.13.2.

leanfran converts the intermediate representation of the Lean compiler into Go.
The generated Go runs with only this module and the Go standard library, so you need neither Lean nor cgo at run time.

[[https://s.conao3.com/blog/2026/21ebbd][The post that introduced leanfran]] covers Rust, Python, TypeScript, and Clojure, and [[https://s.conao3.com/blog/2026/88e5f5][the PHP post]] covers PHP.
The Go version ships from the same repository at the same version.

[[github:conao3/lean-leanfran::Lean][Write and prove functions in Lean 4, run them as Rust, Python, TypeScript, Clojure, PHP and Go]]

** Four ways to use it
There are four ways to use leanfran from Go.

[[./resources/public/img/ad14a8-uses.svg]]

1. Write Lean functions and theorems as the argument of =leanfran.Lean(...)= in a Go package, and call the functions that =go tool leanfran sync= generates from Go.
2. Use Lean structures and inductive types as Go types that come with value checks and JSON conversion.
3. Keep Lean values in Go variables with =leanfran.Value[T]=, and pass them to the next call without converting them.
4. Add =//leanfran:model= to a function written in Go to translate it into Lean, and check the Lean theorems that prove its properties with =go tool leanfran check=.

1 to 3 go from Lean to Go, and 4 goes from Go to Lean.

** Writing Lean in a Go package
Install =leanfran-go=, the CLI that converts Lean code, with nix, and add the leanfran-go package and the command you call with =go tool= to your application's module.

#+begin_src console
$ nix profile install github:conao3/lean-leanfran/v0.13.2#go
$ go mod init example.com/shop
$ go get github.com/conao3/leanfran-go@v0.13.2
$ go get -tool github.com/conao3/leanfran-go/cmd/leanfran@v0.13.2
#+end_src

You need Go 1.26 or later.
Generating code and checking proofs also need =lean= and =lake= from Lean 4.35.0 on your =PATH=.

Write the following package in =pricing/pricing.go=.

#+begin_src go
package pricing

import "github.com/conao3/leanfran-go"

var _ = leanfran.Lean(`
structure Range where
  lo : Nat
  hi : Nat
  ok : lo ≤ hi

def width (r : Range) : Nat := r.hi - r.lo

theorem width_le (r : Range) : width r ≤ r.hi := by
  unfold width
  omega
`)
#+end_src

You write the Lean source as a raw string in =leanfran.Lean(...)=, and this post calls the Lean code you pass to =leanfran.Lean(...)= a block.
Each package holds one block.

The =ok= field of =Range= states that =lo ≤ hi= holds.
=width_le= is a theorem that the width is at most the upper bound.

The caller, =main.go=, creates a value with the generated =NewRange= and passes it to =pricing.Width=.

#+begin_src go
package main

import (
	"fmt"
	"log"
	"math/big"

	"example.com/shop/pricing"
)

func main() {
	r, err := pricing.NewRange(big.NewInt(2), big.NewInt(5))
	if err != nil {
		log.Fatal(err)
	}
	width, err := pricing.Width(r)
	if err != nil {
		log.Fatal(err)
	}
	fmt.Println(width)
}
#+end_src

Run =go tool leanfran sync=, and Lean checks the theorem and leanfran generates Go.
From then on, you can build and run the program with Go alone.

#+begin_src console
$ go tool leanfran sync
leanfran: 1 block checked and generated
$ go run .
3
#+end_src

=sync= writes =leanfran.json=, which records the hash of the block, and the generated Go files to the directory that holds =pricing.go=.
If you commit these files to the repository, CI can run =go tool leanfran status= without Lean to check that they are up to date.

If you change the theorem to =width r ≤ r.lo=, the proof fails and generation stops there.

#+begin_src console
$ go tool leanfran sync 2>&1 | sed "s|$PWD/||"
leanfran: lake build: exit status 1
✖ [4/6] Building LeanGoEmbed.B6578616d706c652e636f6d2f73686f702f70726963696e67 (263ms)
pricing/pricing.go:15:3: error: (lean block example.com/shop/pricing, Lean 11:2) omega could not prove the goal:
a possible counterexample may satisfy the constraints
  b ≥ 0
  a ≥ 0
  a - b ≤ 0
  2*a - b ≤ -1
where
 a := ↑r.lo
 b := ↑r.hi
Some required targets logged failures:
- LeanGoEmbed.B6578616d706c652e636f6d2f73686f702f70726963696e67
error: build failed
#+end_src

The error starts with the line and column in the Go file, followed by the line and column of the Lean code inside the block.
A failed generation leaves the Go that leanfran generated before in place, so =go run .= still prints =3=.

** Lean types become Go types
=Range= becomes a Go struct, and =lo= and =hi= become its fields =Lo= and =Hi= of type =*big.Int=.
=ok= becomes a check of =lo ≤ hi= when you create a value.

The following =cmd/rangecheck/main.go= creates a value from JSON, passes input that breaks the condition to =NewRange=, and then prints the JSON Schema.

#+begin_src go
package main

import (
	"encoding/json"
	"fmt"
	"log"
	"math/big"

	"example.com/shop/pricing"
)

func main() {
	var r pricing.Range
	if err := json.Unmarshal([]byte(`{"lo":1,"hi":4}`), &r); err != nil {
		log.Fatal(err)
	}
	fmt.Println(r.Hi)

	_, err := pricing.NewRange(big.NewInt(5), big.NewInt(2))
	fmt.Println(err)

	schema, err := r.JSONSchema("draft-2020-12")
	if err != nil {
		log.Fatal(err)
	}
	out, _ := json.MarshalIndent(schema, "", "  ")
	fmt.Println(string(out))
}
#+end_src

#+begin_src console
$ go run ./cmd/rangecheck
4
Range.ok: lo ≤ hi
{
  "$schema": "https://json-schema.org/draft/2020-12/schema",
  "additionalProperties": false,
  "properties": {
    "hi": {
      "minimum": 0,
      "type": "integer"
    },
    "lo": {
      "minimum": 0,
      "type": "integer"
    }
  },
  "required": [
    "lo",
    "hi"
  ],
  "type": "object"
}
#+end_src

=NewRange= decides =lo ≤ hi= with code compiled from Lean, so when you pass a =lo= greater than =hi=, it returns a =*leanfran.ValidationError=.
JSON Schema can't express =lo ≤ hi= across two fields, so the schema only states that each =Nat= is 0 or more.

=json.Unmarshal= and =Validate= check the same condition as =NewRange=.
The generated functions also check their arguments when they receive them, so passing a value built with a struct literal to =pricing.Width= returns a =*leanfran.ValidationError= as well.

** Keeping Lean values in Go
On each call, a generated function converts its arguments to Lean's representation and its return value to a Go value.
If you pass a large value again and again, this conversion takes up most of the run time.

=leanfran.Value[T]= is a handle that holds one reference to a Lean value.
With handles, you can keep Lean values in Go variables without converting them.

In =ledger/ledger.go=, write =record=, which appends one amount to an array, and =count=, which returns the number of entries.

#+begin_src go
package ledger

import "github.com/conao3/leanfran-go"

var _ = leanfran.Lean(`
def record (xs : Array UInt64) (x : UInt64) : Array UInt64 := xs.push x

def count (xs : Array UInt64) : Nat := xs.size

theorem count_record (xs : Array UInt64) (x : UInt64) :
    count (record xs x) = count xs + 1 := by
  simp [count, record]
`)
#+end_src

Along with =Record=, which takes a =[]uint64=, =sync= generates =Handle.Record=, which takes a handle and returns a handle.
To convert between Go values and handles, use the methods of the generated =ledger.Value=, such as =ledger.Value.NewArrayUInt64= and =ledger.Value.ReadNat=.

The following =cmd/ledger/main.go= turns the first two entries from a Go slice into a handle, and then adds the next two entries to the handle =entries=.
=record= and =count= don't check their arguments and can't fail on the Lean side, so the generated functions don't return an =error=.

#+begin_src go
package main

import (
	"fmt"

	"example.com/shop/ledger"
)

func main() {
	entries := ledger.Value.NewArrayUInt64([]uint64{1200, 800})
	defer func() { entries.Close() }()

	for _, amount := range []uint64{300, 50} {
		x := ledger.Value.NewUInt64(amount)
		entries = ledger.Handle.Record(entries.Take(), x.Take())
	}

	n := ledger.Handle.Count(entries.Borrow())
	defer n.Close()
	fmt.Println(ledger.Value.ReadNat(n))
	fmt.Println(ledger.Value.ReadArrayUInt64(entries))
}
#+end_src

#+begin_src console
$ go tool leanfran sync
leanfran: 2 blocks checked and generated
$ go run ./cmd/ledger
4
[1200 800 300 50]
#+end_src

Pass =entries.Borrow()= or =entries.Take()= as the argument.
Use =Borrow= when you keep using =entries= after the call, and =Take= when you hand the reference over to Lean and are done with that handle.

No other reference points to the array you pass with =Take=, so Lean's =Array.push= adds the entry in place without copying the array.

=Value.ReadNat= and =Value.ReadArrayUInt64= are the methods that convert the contents of a handle to Go values.
Call =Close= on a handle you are done with to release its reference.
Go's GC doesn't release this reference, so call =Close= on each handle you didn't pass with =Take=.

I measured appending one entry to arrays of 10, 1,000, and 100,000 entries on Linux/amd64 with an Intel Core i5-8400 and Go 1.27.3.
I passed the same slice to =Record= on each call, and kept passing =Handle.Record= a handle that I built from an array of the same size, with =Take=.

The figure and the table show calls per second, computed from the median of 11 runs pinned to one CPU, and higher is better.

[[./resources/public/img/ad14a8-record.svg]]

| Array size | =Record= (calls/s) | =Handle.Record= (calls/s) |
|---+---+---|
| 10 | 2,520,000 | 7,000,000 |
| 1,000 | 63,800 | 7,100,000 |
| 100,000 | 534 | 6,970,000 |

=Record= gets slower as the array grows, while =Handle.Record= stays between 6.97 and 7.10 million calls per second at all three sizes.

Each handle belongs to a region, and the leanfran-go runtime runs operations on handles in the same region one at a time.
The handles in the examples so far belong to the default region, and each process has one default region.
If you create a region with =leanfran.NewRegion()= and create handles inside that region's =WithValues=, multiple goroutines can operate on handles in different regions at the same time.

[[https://github.com/conao3/lean-leanfran/tree/v0.13.2/langs/Go/samples/value-server][The value-server sample]] shows a server that keeps its state in a handle and replaces it with a handle for the next state on each request.

** Proving Go functions in Lean
For the other direction, write =Clamp=, which keeps a value within a range, in Go, and tie it to a Lean specification with =//leanfran:model=.

#+begin_src go
package calc

import "github.com/conao3/leanfran-go"

var _ = leanfran.Lean(`
def clampSpec (x lo hi : Int64) : Int64 := max lo (min hi x)
def ordered (_x lo hi : Int64) : Bool := decide (lo ≤ hi)
def inRange (_x lo hi r : Int64) : Bool := decide (lo ≤ r) && decide (r ≤ hi)
`)

//leanfran:model refines=clampSpec requires=ordered ensures=in_range:inRange
func Clamp(x, lo, hi int64) int64 {
	if x < lo {
		return lo
	}
	if x > hi {
		return hi
	}
	return x
}
#+end_src

=refines= names a Lean function that returns the same value as the implementation, =requires= names the precondition on the inputs, and =ensures= names the condition the return value satisfies.
In this example, the proof obligations are that =Clamp= returns the same value as =clampSpec= when =lo ≤ hi=, and that the return value is at least =lo= and at most =hi=.

=go tool leanfran check= reads the Go syntax tree and types, translates the function into a Lean function, and states the obligations as propositions with names such as =Clamp.obligation.refines=.
The proofs go in =lean/Proofs/= next to =go.mod=, and here I take [[https://github.com/conao3/lean-leanfran/blob/v0.13.2/langs/Go/samples/verified-clamp/lean/Proofs/Clamp.lean][the proof from the verified-clamp sample]] and change only the module name to match this package.

#+begin_src lean
import LeanGoModel.B6578616d706c652e636f6d2f73686f702f63616c63

open LeanGoEmbed.B6578616d706c652e636f6d2f73686f702f63616c63
namespace LeanGoModel.B6578616d706c652e636f6d2f73686f702f63616c63

theorem Clamp.proof.refines : Clamp.obligation.refines := by
  intro x lo hi h
  simp only [ordered, decide_eq_true_eq] at h
  simp only [Clamp, clampSpec, Id.run, pure, Pure.pure, Int64.min_def, Int64.max_def,
    decide_eq_true_eq]
  repeat' split
  all_goals simp_all only [Int64.lt_iff_toInt_lt, Int64.le_iff_toInt_le, ← Int64.toInt_inj] <;> omega

theorem Clamp.proof.in_range : Clamp.obligation.in_range := by
  intro x lo hi h
  simp only [ordered, decide_eq_true_eq] at h
  simp only [Clamp, inRange, Id.run, pure, Pure.pure, Bool.and_eq_true, decide_eq_true_eq]
  split <;> try split
  all_goals simp_all only [Int64.lt_iff_toInt_lt, Int64.le_iff_toInt_le]
  all_goals constructor <;> first | exact True.intro | omega

end LeanGoModel.B6578616d706c652e636f6d2f73686f702f63616c63
#+end_src

The part of the module name after =B= is the Go import path =example.com/shop/calc=, with each UTF-8 byte written in hexadecimal.

#+begin_src console
$ go tool leanfran check --require proved
leanfran: 3 blocks checked and generated
example.com/shop/calc.Clamp [in_range]: proved
example.com/shop/calc.Clamp [refines]: proved
#+end_src

With =--require proved=, the exit code is 1 if any obligation is not =proved=.
=proved= means that the theorem's type matches the obligation and that the proof doesn't rely on =sorry=, which skips a proof, or on axioms outside Lean's standard ones.

=check= writes the result of each obligation to =leanfran.lock= next to =go.mod=, so if you commit that file too, =go tool leanfran status= can check without Lean that the proof results are up to date.

You can also compare the Go implementation with the Lean specification in a test with random inputs, and this test runs without Lean.
=sync= generates =leanfran_model_test.go= in each package that has =//leanfran:model=, so you run the test with =go test=.

#+begin_src console
$ go test ./calc/
ok  	example.com/shop/calc	0.003s
#+end_src

The generated test builds inputs from random numbers with a fixed seed and from boundary values such as 0 and the largest integer, and collects 200 inputs that satisfy =requires=.
For each input, it compares the return value of Go's =Clamp= with the value of =ClampSpec=, the function that leanfran generates from =clampSpec=.

Now change the second =if= in the implementation so that it returns =hi - 1= when =x= is at least =hi=.

#+begin_src go
	if x >= hi {
		return hi - 1
	}
#+end_src

Both proofs fail, so =check= prints Lean's errors to standard error and sets the status of each obligation to =failed=.

#+begin_src console
$ go tool leanfran check --require proved 2>/dev/null
leanfran: 3 blocks checked and generated
example.com/shop/calc.Clamp [in_range]: failed
example.com/shop/calc.Clamp [refines]: failed
#+end_src

The random test that =go test= runs also finds a counterexample, an input where all three arguments are 0.

#+begin_src console
$ go test ./calc/
--- FAIL: TestLeanfranModels (0.00s)
    --- FAIL: TestLeanfranModels/Clamp (0.00s)
        leanfran_model_test.go:12: Clamp: refines: got []interface {}{-1}, want []interface {}{0} (seed=1, input=[]interface {}{0, 0, 0})
FAIL
FAIL	example.com/shop/calc	0.002s
FAIL
#+end_src

** What the proofs guarantee
The Lean theorems guarantee properties of the functions written in Lean and of the Lean models translated from Go.
For those properties to hold when the generated Go or the original Go runs, the generator and the runtime that convert Lean to Go, the translator that turns Go into Lean, and the model of Go's operations must be correct, so I check these four parts with tests.

I check the translator with tests that compare the results of running hand-written Go with the results of compiling the translated model with Lean's standard C backend and running it.
For the model of operations, tests compare code generated from the model with Go's operations at boundary values, and also check that each failure in the model matches a =panic= in Go.

I check the generator and the runtime that convert Lean to Go with tests that compare the results of the generated Go with those of Lean's C backend.

At the time of writing, I have tried 1,769,817 numeric operations built from boundary values and random numbers on Linux/amd64.
Of those, 1,764,071 results match the C backend byte for byte.

The remaining 5,746 come from functions that return floating-point numbers, and their differences stay within a tolerance set for each function.
=Float.cos= differs the most, by 88 times the gap between adjacent floating-point numbers.

In the translation from Go to Lean, leanfran maps Go integers to Lean integers of the same width, and =int= and =uint= to =Int64= and =UInt64=.
Division by zero, out-of-range indexes, and =panic= become values that represent failure in the model.

leanfran can translate a subset of Go: =if=, =switch=, =for=, slice indexing and =append=, and structs.

Functions that use pointers, maps, channels, goroutines, methods, generics, =defer=, or input and output are out of scope.
The full list of supported syntax is in [[https://github.com/conao3/lean-leanfran/blob/v0.13.2/docs/go-guide.md#go-subset-and-proof-scope][the Go guide]].

** Wrapping up
Besides the examples in this post, [[https://github.com/conao3/lean-leanfran/tree/v0.13.2/langs/Go/samples][the Go samples]] include verified-nibble, which proves that a bit mask gives the same result as a remainder.
There are also embed-models, which shares a Go struct between two packages, and greet-cli, which runs a Lean =IO= function as a Go command.

The setup steps are in [[https://github.com/conao3/lean-leanfran/blob/v0.13.2/langs/Go/README.md][the Go README]], and the details of the type mapping and the CLI are in [[https://github.com/conao3/lean-leanfran/blob/v0.13.2/docs/go-guide.md][the Go guide]].

* A Clojure core cheat sheet in math notation
:properties:
:export_file_name: generated/contents/blog/2026/315a71
:export_date: 2026-11-25 01:17
:export_updated: 2026-11-25 01:17
:export_lang: en
:export_tags: clojure standard-library
:end:

I wrote down 163 functions from =clojure.core= that work on sequences, collections and functions, each as a small formula.
I borrowed the notation from Daniel Keep's [[https://danielkeep.github.io/itercheat_baked.html][Rust Iterator Cheat Sheet]] (CC BY-SA 4.0) and moved it to Clojure syntax, with seqs, vectors, maps and sets written as Clojure literals and function calls written as lists.
The rows describe Clojure 1.12.7.
A [[https://github.com/conao3/blog-stasis-src/blob/master/bin/315a71-clojure-cheatsheet.clj][script]] keeps every row next to 333 checks that run the function in Clojure, and it builds the tables only when all of the checks pass.

** Reading the notation

The figure reads the =take-while= row, and then follows the same row through =(take-while #(< % 3) (range))=.

[[./resources/public/img/315a71-reading-a-row.svg]]

- \((a_0\ a_1\ \ldots)\) is a seq. \(a\) and \(b\) are input seqs, and a subscript picks one element.
- \(\texttt{'}(a_0\ a_1\ \ldots)\) is a list, \([a_0\ a_1\ \ldots]\) is a vector, \(\{k_0\ v_0,\ \ldots\}\) is a map, and \(\#\{a_0\ \ldots\}\) is a set, as in Clojure source. The list rows of =peek= and =pop= need a real list, and a seq such as the result of =map= throws there.
- \((f\ a_0)\) calls \(f\) with \(a_0\), as in Clojure source.
- \(f\), \(g\) and \(h\) are functions that compute new values, and \(\mathit{keyfn}\) is a key function such as the one =sort-by= takes.
- \(p\) and \(q\) are predicates. A predicate result counts as \(\mathtt{true}\) when it is anything other than \(\mathtt{nil}\) or \(\mathtt{false}\).
- \(c\) is a comparator, such as =compare= or =>=.
- \(f : x\ y \to z\) says that \(f\) takes two arguments, and \(\text{bool}\) and \(\text{number}\) name the kind of value it returns. \(\mathit{acc}\) is the accumulated value of a reducing function, and \(\mathit{init}\) is its first value.
- \(\mathit{xf}\) is a transducer, such as =(map inc)=.
- \(i\) and \(j\) are positions, except in =range=, where they are the start and end values. \(n\) is a count that you pass in, \(s\) is a step, and \(l\) and \(l'\) are the lengths of the input seqs.
- \(m\) is a map, \(k\) is a key, \(v\) and \(w\) are values, and \(d\) is a default value.
- \(x \mapsto (f\ x)\) is a function, the same as =(fn [x] (f x))=. \((x_0\ \ldots) \mapsto \ldots\) takes any number of arguments.
- A superscript ! marks a transient, as in \([a_0\ \ldots]^{!}\).
- \(\sigma\) is a permutation of the positions, and "wh." reads "where". Other letters name values that appear in the arguments or that the row defines after "wh.".
- An underlined element stays unrealized after you call the function and consume every seq in its result. =(take-while p a)= has to look at \(a_i\) to know where to stop, so I underline only the elements after \(a_i\). I measured this on an unchunked lazy seq. Over a vector or a finite =range=, many lazy functions such as =map= and =filter= compute 32 results at a time, because vectors and finite ranges give chunked seqs.
- A check in the Lazy column means the function returns a lazy seq, which computes its elements when you ask for them.
- A check in the xf column means the function returns a [[https://clojure.org/reference/transducers][transducer]] when you call it without the collection, as in =(map inc)=.
- The function name links to its entry in the [[https://clojure.github.io/clojure/clojure.core-api.html][clojure.core API reference]].

** How I grouped the functions

The [[https://clojure.org/api/cheatsheet][official Clojure cheat sheet]] groups its "Seq in, Seq out" functions under headings such as "Get shorter", "Get longer", "Head-items", "Tail-items" and "'Change'".
Some functions sit under two of those headings, such as =filter=, which appears under "Get shorter" and "'Change'".

I grouped each function by how the elements of its result relate to the elements of its input, so each function appears once.
- Selecting: every result element is an input element, in the input order.
- Transforming: the result elements are values that \(f\) computes from the input elements.
- Combining: the result adds elements to a seq, or joins several seqs or nested collections into one seq.
- Reordering: the result has the same elements in another order.
- Splitting: the result holds the input elements in groups.
- Reducing: the result is one value.
- Collecting: the result is a vector, a set, a map, or the collection you pass to =into=.

Rich Hickey described the argument order of =clojure.core= in [[https://groups.google.com/g/clojure/c/iyyNyWs53dc][a mailing list thread]] in 2008:

#+begin_quote
Sequence functions take their sources last and collection functions take their primary operand (collection) first.
#+end_quote

Most functions in the groups above are sequence functions, so the seq comes last and they work with =->>=.
=nth=, =nthrest= and =nthnext= take the seq first, and =max-key= and =min-key= take values instead of a seq.
The functions that read or update a vector, map or set take it first and work with =->=.
After them come the functions that build collections, test what kind of collection a value is, work on transients, and compare values.

** Making a seq

These functions make a seq from nothing, from a value or from a collection.
Without a transducer, =sequence= only turns its argument into a seq, so a vector gives a chunked seq and a lazy seq comes back as it is.

#+INCLUDE: "generated/include/315a71/making.html" export html

** Selecting by position

These functions keep or drop elements by counting.
=rest= returns an empty seq when nothing is left, and =next= returns \(\mathtt{nil}\), so =next= has to realize one more element to find out.

#+INCLUDE: "generated/include/315a71/position.html" export html

** Selecting by predicate

These functions keep or drop elements by testing each one, or by comparing it with the elements before it.

#+INCLUDE: "generated/include/315a71/predicate.html" export html

** Transforming

These functions compute new elements from the input elements.
With more than one input seq, =map= stops at the end of the shortest one.

#+INCLUDE: "generated/include/315a71/transforming.html" export html

** Combining

=interleave= stops at the end of the shortest seq, and =flatten= replaces each nested sequential collection, such as a vector or a list, with its elements.

#+INCLUDE: "generated/include/315a71/combining.html" export html

** Reordering

=sort= and =sort-by= are stable, so equal elements keep their input order.

#+INCLUDE: "generated/include/315a71/reordering.html" export html

** Splitting

=partition= and its relatives return a seq of groups, and =split-at=, =split-with= and =splitv-at= return a vector of two parts.

#+INCLUDE: "generated/include/315a71/splitting.html" export html

** Reducing to a value

These functions consume a seq and return one value.
=some=, =every?=, =not-every?= and =not-any?= stop at the first element that decides the answer.
=transduce= calls \(f\) with one argument at the end, and =completing= adds that arity to a two-argument function.

#+INCLUDE: "generated/include/315a71/reducing.html" export html

** Collecting into a collection

The result is a vector, a set or a map that holds the elements of the seq, or the collection you pass to =into= with the elements added.

#+INCLUDE: "generated/include/315a71/collecting.html" export html

** Collections

These functions take the collection first.
=conj= adds at the end of a vector and at the front of a list.
=assoc=, =dissoc=, =conj=, =merge= and =empty= keep the type of their first argument, such as a sorted map, and =select-keys=, =update-keys= and =update-vals= return a plain map.

#+INCLUDE: "generated/include/315a71/collections.html" export html

** Constructing collections

These functions build a collection from the values you pass.
=array-map= keeps the keys in the given order until you =assoc= more keys onto a map that has more than 8 entries, which turns it into a hash map.
The sorted variants keep their keys ordered by =compare= or by the comparator you pass.

#+INCLUDE: "generated/include/315a71/constructing.html" export html

** Predicates on collections

Each predicate tells you what kind of collection a value is.
A Clojure map entry is a vector of a key and a value, so =vector?=, =sequential?= and =indexed?= return true for it.

#+INCLUDE: "generated/include/315a71/predicates.html" export html

** Transients

A [[https://clojure.org/reference/transients][transient]] is a version of a vector, hash map or hash set that you make in constant time, change with the functions that end in =!=, and turn back into a persistent collection.
Each of those functions returns the updated transient, and you keep using that return value.
Sorted collections and lists have no transient version.

#+INCLUDE: "generated/include/315a71/transients.html" export html

** Comparing and testing values

~=~ compares values, so a vector and a list with the same elements are equal, and =identical?= compares objects.
~(= 1 1.0)~ is false, because integers and floating-point numbers are never ~=~ to each other; ~(== 1 1.0)~ compares them as numbers.
=compare= is the default order of =sort= and the sorted collections.
It orders numbers by value across types, so =(compare 1 1.0)= is 0, and it orders vectors by length first and then element by element.
Lists, sets and maps do not implement =Comparable=, and =compare= throws on them.

#+INCLUDE: "generated/include/315a71/values.html" export html

** Functions

Each function here builds, calls or wraps functions.

#+INCLUDE: "generated/include/315a71/functions.html" export html

** Related functions without a formula

These functions control when Clojure realizes a seq, run side effects, or help you write transducers, so I describe them in words.

| Function        | What it does                                                                                       |
|-----------------+----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| =doall=         | Realizes a lazy seq and returns it.                                                                |
| =dorun=         | Realizes a lazy seq for its side effects and returns =nil=.                                        |
| =run!=          | Calls a function on each element for its side effects and returns =nil=.                          |
| =doseq=         | A macro that runs a body for each element, with the bindings of =for=.                            |
| =for=           | A macro for list comprehension that returns a lazy seq.                                            |
| =realized?=     | Tells whether a lazy seq, delay, future or promise already has its value.                         |
| =lazy-seq=      | A macro that makes a lazy seq from a body that returns a seq.                                      |
| =lazy-cat=      | A macro version of =concat= that evaluates each collection expression only when needed.           |
| =iteration=     | Makes a seqable and reducible value from repeated calls to a step function, such as fetching pages of an API. |
| =tree-seq=      | Walks a tree depth first and returns the nodes as a lazy seq.                                     |
| =eduction=      | Applies transducers to a collection each time you reduce or iterate it.                           |
| =cat=           | A transducer that concatenates the collections it receives.                                        |
| =halt-when=     | Returns a transducer that stops the reduction at the first input that satisfies a predicate.      |
| =completing=    | Adds a completion arity to a reducing function, for use with =transduce=.                         |
| =reduced=       | Wraps a value so that =reduce= stops and returns it.                                               |
| =bounded-count= | Counts the elements of a seq, stopping after a given number.                                       |
| =reduced?=      | Tells whether a value is wrapped by =reduced=.                                                     |
| =unreduced=     | Takes the value out of a =reduced= wrapper, and returns other values as they are.                  |
| =ensure-reduced= | Wraps a value with =reduced= unless it is wrapped already.                                        |
| =seque=         | Makes a queued seq that realizes another seq in the background, up to n items ahead of the consumer. |
| =iterator-seq=  | Makes a seq from a =java.util.Iterator=.                                                           |
| =enumeration-seq= | Makes a seq from a =java.util.Enumeration=.                                                      |
| =line-seq=      | Makes a lazy seq of the lines read from a =java.io.BufferedReader=.                               |
| =file-seq=      | Walks a directory tree and returns its =java.io.File= objects as a lazy seq.                      |
| =xml-seq=       | Walks a tree parsed by =clojure.xml/parse= and returns its elements and text nodes as a lazy seq. |
| =resultset-seq= | Makes a lazy seq of maps from the rows of a =java.sql.ResultSet=.                                  |
| =to-array=      | Copies a collection into a Java =Object[]=.                                                        |
| =to-array-2d=   | Copies a collection of collections into a Java =Object[][]=.                                       |
| =into-array=    | Copies a seq into a Java array of a given element type, or of the first element's type.           |
| =deref=         | Reads the value of a reference such as an atom, a delay, a future or a promise; =@x= is short for it. |
| =bean=          | Makes a read-only map view of a Java object from its JavaBean properties.                         |

I left out the rest of =clojure.core=, which includes numbers, strings, concurrency, namespaces, macros for control flow and the other parts of Java interop.

* clojure.coreの関数を数式で表したClojureのチートシート
:properties:
:export_file_name: generated/contents/blog/2026/76293c
:export_original: /blog/2026/315a71
:export_date: 2026-11-27 20:55
:export_updated: 2026-11-27 20:55
:export_tags: clojure standard-library
:export_draft: t
:end:

Clojureの =clojure.core= のうちseqとコレクションと関数を扱う163個の関数を、1つずつ小さな式で書いたチートシートを作りました。
記法はDaniel Keepさんの [[https://danielkeep.github.io/itercheat_baked.html][Rust Iterator Cheat Sheet]] (CC BY-SA 4.0) から借りてClojureの構文に移し、seqとベクターとマップとセットをClojureのリテラルで、関数の呼び出しをリストで書いています。
表の内容はClojure 1.12.7のものです。
表を書き出す [[https://github.com/conao3/blog-stasis-src/blob/master/bin/315a71-clojure-cheatsheet.clj][スクリプト]] は各行と、その関数をClojureで動かす333個の検査を並べて持っていて、検査がすべて通ったときだけ表を作ります。

** 記法の読み方

図で =take-while= の行を読み、続けて同じ行を =(take-while #(< % 3) (range))= でたどります。

[[./resources/public/img/315a71-reading-a-row.svg]]

- \((a_0\ a_1\ \ldots)\)はseqです。
  \(a\)と\(b\)は入力のseqで、添字で要素を1つ選びます。
- \(\texttt{'}(a_0\ a_1\ \ldots)\)はリスト、\([a_0\ a_1\ \ldots]\)はベクター、\(\{k_0\ v_0,\ \ldots\}\)はマップ、\(\#\{a_0\ \ldots\}\)はセットで、Clojureのソースと同じ書き方です。
  =peek= と =pop= のリストの行には本物のリストが要り、 =map= の結果のようなseqを渡すと =peek= と =pop= は例外を投げます。
- \((f\ a_0)\)はClojureのソースと同じ書き方で、\(f\)を\(a_0\)で呼ぶことを表します。
- \(f\)と\(g\)と\(h\)は新しい値を計算する関数で、\(\mathit{keyfn}\)は =sort-by= が受け取るようなキーの関数です。
- \(p\)と\(q\)は述語です。
  述語の結果は\(\mathtt{nil}\)でも\(\mathtt{false}\)でもなければ\(\mathtt{true}\)とみなします。
- \(c\)は =compare= や =>= のような比較関数です。
- \(f : x\ y \to z\)は\(f\)が引数を2つ取ることを表し、\(\text{bool}\)と\(\text{number}\)は返す値の種類を表します。
  \(\mathit{acc}\)はreduceする関数の累積値で、\(\mathit{init}\)はその最初の値です。
- \(\mathit{xf}\)は =(map inc)= のようなトランスデューサーです。
- \(i\)と\(j\)は位置を表し、 =range= では始まりと終わりの値を表します。
  \(n\)は渡す個数、\(s\)は刻み幅、\(l\)と\(l'\)は入力のseqの長さです。
- \(m\)はマップ、\(k\)はキー、\(v\)と\(w\)は値、\(d\)は既定値です。
- \(x \mapsto (f\ x)\)は関数で、 =(fn [x] (f x))= と同じです。
  \((x_0\ \ldots) \mapsto \ldots\)は任意の個数の引数を取ります。
- \([a_0\ \ldots]^{!}\)のように上付きの!を付けたものはtransientです。
- \(\sigma\)は位置の置換です。
  図のwh.と表の「ただし」の後には値の定義や条件が続き、ほかの文字は引数に出てくる値か、その行が「ただし」の後で定義する値です。
- 下線を引いた要素は関数を呼んで結果のseqをすべて消費しても実体化しません。
  下線の位置はチャンク化されていない遅延seqで測っていて、 =(take-while p a)= は止まる場所を知るために\(a_i\)を見る必要があるので\(a_i\)より後の要素にだけ下線を引いています。
  ベクターと有限の =range= から作るチャンク化されたseqでは、 =map= や =filter= のような多くの遅延の関数が結果を32個ずつ計算します。
- 遅延の列に印のある関数は遅延seqを返し、要素を求められたときに計算します。
- xfの列に印のある関数は、 =(map inc)= のようにコレクションを渡さずに呼ぶと [[https://clojure.org/reference/transducers][トランスデューサー]] を返します。
- 関数の名前は [[https://clojure.github.io/clojure/clojure.core-api.html][clojure.core API reference]] のその関数の項へリンクしています。

** 関数の分け方

Clojureの [[https://clojure.org/api/cheatsheet][公式のチートシート]] は「Seq in, Seq out」の関数を「Get shorter」「Get longer」「Head-items」「Tail-items」「'Change'」のような見出しで分けています。
2つの見出しに入っている関数もあり、たとえば =filter= は「Get shorter」と「'Change'」にあります。

私は結果の要素と入力の要素の関係で関数を分けたので、どの関数も1回だけ出てきます。
- 選ぶ関数の結果は入力の要素を入力の順に持ちます。
- 変換する関数の結果は、\(f\)が入力の要素から計算した値を持ちます。
- つなぐ関数の結果はseqに要素を足すか、複数のseqや入れ子のコレクションを1つのseqにつなげたものです。
- 並べ替える関数の結果は同じ要素を別の順に並べたものです。
- 分ける関数の結果は入力の要素を組に分けて持ちます。
- まとめる関数の結果は1つの値です。
- 集める関数の結果はベクター、セット、マップ、 =into= に渡したコレクションのどれかです。

Rich Hickeyさんは2008年の [[https://groups.google.com/g/clojure/c/iyyNyWs53dc][メーリングリストのスレッド]] で、 =clojure.core= の引数の順を次のように説明しました。

#+begin_quote
Sequence functions take their sources last and collection functions take their primary operand (collection) first.
#+end_quote

上の分類の関数のほとんどは引用のsequence functionsに当たるので、seqを最後に取って =->>= で使えます。
=nth= と =nthrest= と =nthnext= はseqを最初に取り、 =max-key= と =min-key= はseqの代わりに値を取ります。

ベクターやマップやセットを読んだり更新したりする関数はコレクションを最初に取り、 =->= で使えます。
その後に、コレクションを作る関数、値がどの種類のコレクションかを調べる関数、transientを扱う関数、値を比べる関数が続きます。

** seqを作る

これらの関数は何もないところや1つの値やコレクションからseqを作ります。
トランスデューサーを渡さないと =sequence= は引数をseqにするだけなので、ベクターからはチャンク化されたseqができ、遅延seqはそのまま返ります。

#+INCLUDE: "generated/include/315a71/ja/making.html" export html

** 位置で選ぶ

これらの関数は個数を数えて要素を残したり捨てたりします。
=rest= は何も残らないと空のseqを返し、 =next= は\(\mathtt{nil}\)を返します。
=next= は残りがあるかを知るために、要素をもう1つ実体化する必要があります。

#+INCLUDE: "generated/include/315a71/ja/position.html" export html

** 述語で選ぶ

これらの関数は要素を1つずつ調べるか前の要素と比べて、残すか捨てるかを決めます。

#+INCLUDE: "generated/include/315a71/ja/predicate.html" export html

** 変換する

これらの関数は入力の要素から新しい要素を計算します。
入力のseqが2つ以上あるとき、 =map= は一番短いseqの終わりで止まります。

#+INCLUDE: "generated/include/315a71/ja/transforming.html" export html

** つなぐ

=interleave= は一番短いseqの終わりで止まります。
=flatten= はベクターやリストのような入れ子のシーケンシャルなコレクションを、その要素で置き換えます。

#+INCLUDE: "generated/include/315a71/ja/combining.html" export html

** 並べ替える

=sort= と =sort-by= は安定なので、等しい要素は入力の順を保ちます。

#+INCLUDE: "generated/include/315a71/ja/reordering.html" export html

** 分ける

=partition= で始まる関数は組のseqを返し、 =split-at= と =split-with= と =splitv-at= は2つの部分のベクターを返します。

#+INCLUDE: "generated/include/315a71/ja/splitting.html" export html

** 1つの値にまとめる

これらの関数はseqを消費して1つの値を返します。
=some= と =every?= と =not-every?= と =not-any?= は、答えが決まった最初の要素で止まります。

=transduce= は最後に\(f\)を引数1つで呼び、 =completing= は2引数の関数にそのアリティを足します。

#+INCLUDE: "generated/include/315a71/ja/reducing.html" export html

** コレクションに集める

結果はseqの要素を持つベクター、セット、マップのどれかになります。
=into= は渡したコレクションにseqの要素を足します。

#+INCLUDE: "generated/include/315a71/ja/collecting.html" export html

** コレクション

これらの関数はコレクションを最初に取ります。
=conj= はベクターには末尾に、リストには先頭に足します。

=assoc= と =dissoc= と =conj= と =merge= と =empty= はソート済みマップのような最初の引数の型を保ちます。
=select-keys= と =update-keys= と =update-vals= は普通のマップを返します。

#+INCLUDE: "generated/include/315a71/ja/collections.html" export html

** コレクションを作る

これらの関数は渡した値からコレクションを作ります。
=array-map= はキーを渡した順に保ちますが、8個より多いエントリーを持つ =array-map= にさらにキーを =assoc= するとハッシュマップになります。
ソート済みのマップとセットはキーを =compare= か渡した比較関数の順に保ちます。

#+INCLUDE: "generated/include/315a71/ja/constructing.html" export html

** コレクションの述語

どの述語も、値がどの種類のコレクションかを答えます。
Clojureのマップのエントリーはキーと値のベクターなので、 =vector?= と =sequential?= と =indexed?= はそれに対してtrueを返します。

#+INCLUDE: "generated/include/315a71/ja/predicates.html" export html

** transient

ベクターとハッシュマップとハッシュセットには [[https://clojure.org/reference/transients][transient]] があり、定数時間で作って =!= で終わる関数で変更してから、永続コレクションに戻せます。
=!= で終わる関数はどれも更新したtransientを返すので、次の変更にはその戻り値を使います。

ソート済みのコレクションとリストのtransientは作れません。

#+INCLUDE: "generated/include/315a71/ja/transients.html" export html

** 値の比較と判定

~=~ は値を比べるので同じ要素を持つベクターとリストは等しくなり、オブジェクトそのものを比べるときは =identical?= を使います。
整数と浮動小数点数は互いに ~=~ にならないので ~(= 1 1.0)~ はfalseで、 ~(== 1 1.0)~ は数として比べます。

=compare= は =sort= とソート済みのコレクションの既定の順です。
数は型をまたいで値の順に並べるので、 =(compare 1 1.0)= は0になります。

ベクターはまず長さで、次に要素ごとに並べます。
リストとセットとマップは =Comparable= を実装していないので、 =compare= に渡すと例外を投げます。

#+INCLUDE: "generated/include/315a71/ja/values.html" export html

** 関数

この節では関数を作るものや、関数を呼んだり包んだりするものを扱います。

#+INCLUDE: "generated/include/315a71/ja/functions.html" export html

** 式を書かなかった関連の関数

これらの関数はClojureがseqを実体化する時を決めるか、副作用を起こすか、トランスデューサーを書くのを助けるので、言葉で説明します。

| 関数             | 説明                                                                                       |
|------------------+--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| =doall=          | 遅延seqを実体化して返します。                                                              |
| =dorun=          | 遅延seqを副作用のために実体化し、 =nil= を返します。                                       |
| =run!=           | 副作用のために各要素で関数を呼び、 =nil= を返します。                                      |
| =doseq=          | =for= と同じ束縛で、要素ごとに本体を実行するマクロです。                                   |
| =for=            | 遅延seqを返すリスト内包表記のマクロです。                                                  |
| =realized?=      | 遅延seq、delay、future、promiseが値をもう持っているかを答えます。                          |
| =lazy-seq=       | seqを返す本体から遅延seqを作るマクロです。                                                 |
| =lazy-cat=       | 各コレクションの式を必要になったときだけ評価する、マクロ版の =concat= です。              |
| =iteration=      | APIのページを取ってくるようなステップ関数を繰り返し呼んで、seqableでreducibleな値を作ります。 |
| =tree-seq=       | 木を深さ優先でたどり、ノードを遅延seqで返します。                                          |
| =eduction=       | コレクションをreduceするか反復するたびに、トランスデューサーを適用します。                |
| =cat=            | 受け取ったコレクションを連結するトランスデューサーです。                                   |
| =halt-when=      | 述語を満たす最初の入力でreduceを止めるトランスデューサーを返します。                       |
| =completing=     | =transduce= で使えるように、reduceする関数に完了のアリティを足します。                     |
| =reduced=        | 値を包んで、 =reduce= が止まってその値を返すようにします。                                 |
| =bounded-count=  | seqの要素を数え、指定した数に達したら止まります。                                          |
| =reduced?=       | 値が =reduced= で包まれているかを答えます。                                                |
| =unreduced=      | =reduced= の包みから値を取り出し、ほかの値はそのまま返します。                             |
| =ensure-reduced= | 値がまだ包まれていなければ =reduced= で包みます。                                          |
| =seque=          | 別のseqを裏で実体化するキュー付きのseqを作り、消費する側より最大n個先まで進みます。       |
| =iterator-seq=   | =java.util.Iterator= からseqを作ります。                                                    |
| =enumeration-seq= | =java.util.Enumeration= からseqを作ります。                                                |
| =line-seq=       | =java.io.BufferedReader= から読んだ行の遅延seqを作ります。                                 |
| =file-seq=       | ディレクトリの木をたどり、その =java.io.File= のオブジェクトを遅延seqで返します。         |
| =xml-seq=        | =clojure.xml/parse= で読んだ木をたどり、要素とテキストのノードを遅延seqで返します。       |
| =resultset-seq=  | =java.sql.ResultSet= の行からマップの遅延seqを作ります。                                   |
| =to-array=       | コレクションをJavaの =Object[]= に写します。                                               |
| =to-array-2d=    | コレクションのコレクションをJavaの =Object[][]= に写します。                               |
| =into-array=     | seqを、指定した要素の型か最初の要素の型のJavaの配列に写します。                           |
| =deref=          | atom、delay、future、promiseのような参照の値を読み、 =@x= はその略記です。                |
| =bean=           | JavaオブジェクトのJavaBeanのプロパティから、読み取り専用のマップのビューを作ります。       |

数と文字列と並行処理と名前空間、制御のためのマクロ、そのほかのJava相互運用といった残りの =clojure.core= の部分は省きました。
* Lean 4で証明したkernelをRustとPythonとGoのHTTPサーバーにするleangageを作った
:properties:
:export_file_name: generated/contents/blog/2026/a886f0
:export_date: 2026-11-26 13:10
:export_updated: 2026-11-26 13:10
:export_tags: lean rust python go formal-verification code-generation postgresql performance release lean-leangage lean-leanfran
:export_draft: t
:end:
Lean 4で書いて証明した関数を、RustとPythonとGoのHTTPサーバーとして動かすwebフレームワークのleangageを作りました。
サービスのロジックを1つの関数にまとめてLeanで書くと、認可や組織ごとのデータの分離のような性質を定理として証明した関数を、3つの言語のサーバーから呼べます。

リポジトリは[[https://github.com/conao3/lean-leangage][conao3/lean-leangage]]で、ライセンスはApache-2.0です。
パッケージの登録先には出していないので、この記事はリポジトリのcommit [[https://github.com/conao3/lean-leangage/tree/7156538][7156538]]をもとに書いています。

設計は[[https://github.com/h5i-dev/h5i/blob/main/crates/h5i-app/README.md][h5i-app]]を参考にしています。
h5i-appはRustで書いたロジックを[[https://github.com/AeneasVerif/aeneas][Aeneas]]でLeanに訳して証明するフレームワークで、leangageは向きを逆にして、Leanで書いたロジックを各言語に変換します。

[[github:conao3/lean-leangage::Rust][Web services whose core is a kernel proved in Lean 4, generated to Rust, Python and Go with leanfran]]

** kernelとサーバー
leangageではサービスのロジックを書いた関数をkernelと呼びます。
テナントはサービスを使う組織ごとの区画のことで、kernelは1つのテナントの状態だけを見ます。

kernelは呼び出した利用者とテナントの状態と命令の3つを受け取ります。
命令を受け付けるなら状態への書き込みと返信を返し、受け付けないならエラーを返します。

[[./resources/public/img/a886f0-layers.svg]]

Leanにはkernelのほかに、どのサービスでも使う部品が書いてあります。
誰が何を読み書きしてよいかを確かめる認可のguardとSQLのコンパイラとbearer tokenの形式がその部品です。

認証と失敗の返信を決める関数とJSONのトークンを扱う関数とJSONを書く関数も、どのサービスでも使います。

サービスごとにLeanで書くものには、kernelと、要求を命令に直す関数と、kernelの結果を返信に直す関数と、PostgreSQLの表の定義があります。

これらを[[https://s.conao3.com/blog/2026/23d62c][leanfran]]でRustとPythonとGoのコードに変換して、手で書いたサーバーから呼びます。
サーバーが受け持つのはHTTPの受け付けとJSONの読み取りと署名の計算と状態の保存で、状態の置き場所はメモリとPostgreSQLから選べます。

** 電卓のkernelを書く
最初の例は利用者ごとに数を1つ覚えておく電卓で、kernelは[[https://github.com/conao3/lean-leangage/blob/7156538/lean/Calculator/Kernel.lean#L90-L98][lean/Calculator/Kernel.lean]]の =transition= という関数です。
=actor= が呼び出した利用者で、 =snap= がテナントの状態です。

#+begin_src lean
def transition (actor : Principal) (snap : Snapshot) (cmd : Command) :
    Except Error (Option Memory × Reply) :=
  match cmd with
  | .set value => .ok (some { user := actor.user, value }, .value value)
  | .apply op arg =>
    match compute op (memoryOf snap.memories actor.user) arg with
    | .ok v => .ok (some { user := actor.user, value := v }, .value v)
    | .error e => .error e
  | .get => .ok (none, .value (memoryOf snap.memories actor.user))
#+end_src

命令は =set= と =apply= と =get= の3つです。
=set= は数を覚え、 =apply= は覚えている数に演算をして結果を覚え直し、 =get= は覚えている数を返します。

返り値の =Option Memory= は状態に書き込む行で、 =get= のように何も書き込まない命令では =none= になります。
結果が64bitに収まらない演算と、結果が負になる引き算と、0での割り算は =Error= を返して、何も書き込みません。

** kernelの性質を証明する
この関数の性質は[[https://github.com/conao3/lean-leangage/blob/7156538/lean/Calculator/Proofs.lean][lean/Calculator/Proofs.lean]]で証明しています。
たとえば次の =others_unchanged= は、ある利用者の命令がほかの利用者の数を変えないという定理です。

#+begin_src lean
theorem others_unchanged (a : Principal) (s : Snapshot) (c : Command) (w : Option Memory)
    (r : Reply) (ht : transition a s c = .ok (w, r)) (u : UInt64) (hu : u ≠ a.user) :
    memoryOf (apply s w).memories u = memoryOf s.memories u
#+end_src

=memoryOf= は状態から利用者の数を読む関数です。
=apply s w= は書き込みの =w= を状態の =s= に反映するLeanの関数で、命令の =apply= とは別のものです。

仮定の =ht= は命令が受け付けられたことを表し、 =hu= は =u= が呼び出した利用者とは別の利用者であることを表します。
結論は、書き込みを反映したあとの =u= の数が反映する前と同じだという等式です。

どの定理もすべての利用者と状態と命令について述べていて、ほかには次の定理があります。

| 定理 | 内容 |
|---|---|
| =transition_spec= | 返信は、桁の上限がない自然数で同じ計算をした結果と一致し、命令を拒否するのは、結果が64bitに収まらないときと、引き算の結果が負になるときと、0で割るときだけである |
| =get_after= | 受け付けられた命令のあとで同じ利用者が =get= を呼ぶと、その命令の返信と同じ数が返る |
| =read_only_sound= | =get= は何も書き込まない |

** leanfranでRustとPythonとGoに変換する
Leanの関数は、leanfranのコマンドで言語ごとのコードに変換します。
電卓のkernelでは次の3つを実行していて、[[https://github.com/conao3/lean-leangage/blob/7156538/Makefile#L51-L80][Makefile]]の =generate= がまとめて呼びます。

#+begin_src sh
leanfran project generate --lake-dir lean \
  --output-dir rust/calculator/src/generated --modules Calculator.Kernel \
  --output text
leanfran-python module generate --module-name Calculator.Kernel \
  --search-path lean/.lake/build/lib/lean \
  --output-file python/src/leangage_calculator/kernel.py --output text
leanfran-go module generate --module-name Calculator.Kernel \
  --search-path lean/.lake/build/lib/lean --output-dir go/calculator/kernel \
  --output text
#+end_src

leanfranは0.13.2を使っています。
Rustでは、Leanの =transition= が[[https://github.com/conao3/lean-leangage/blob/7156538/rust/calculator/src/generated/calculator_kernel.rs#L4225][次の型の関数]]になります。

#+begin_src rust
pub fn transition(actor: Principal, snap: Snapshot, cmd: Command)
    -> Result<(Option<Memory>, Reply), Error>
#+end_src

Leanの =Except= はRustの =Result= になり、 =Principal= や =Command= は同じ名前のRustの型になります。
変換したコードはリポジトリにcommitしてあって、 =make check= は変換をやり直してcommitしたファイルと差があれば失敗します。

変換したコードがLeanの関数と同じ結果を返すことは、テストで確かめています。
